passage:
March: Hrithik had tried everything he could find on his own: breathing videos, a worry journal, cutting out coffee. He still hadn't taken the metro in four months, and he had just said no to his cousin's wedding in Pune. 'I think I need a proper doctor,' he told Pankaj, and felt oddly lighter for saying it.
April: Pankaj offered to come along. In the clinic waiting room he scrolled on his phone and didn't ask a single question. When Hrithik came out holding a referral to a therapist, Pankaj just said, 'Biryani?'
June: after six sessions, Hrithik rode two metro stops with the therapist's plan folded in his pocket. He texted Pankaj a photo of the station sign. Pankaj replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which was exactly right.

qa.q: What did Hrithik come out of the clinic holding?
qa.a: He came out holding a referral to a therapist.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik feel oddly lighter after telling Pankaj he needed a doctor?
qa.a: Saying it aloud admitted that self-help alone wasn't enough, which seems to have eased the weight of struggling on his own.

qa.q: What did Pankaj get right as a friend?
qa.a: He came along, stayed patient in the waiting room without questioning, and replied simply to the photo, supporting Hrithik without taking over.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pankaj to hold back his questions?
qa.a: Pankaj may be curious and worried, but not asking lets Hrithik own the process, which probably takes some patience.

grounding: It shows a young man whose anxiety keeps limiting his life seeing a doctor and therapist, with a friend who is patient without taking over.

passage:
Ayesha pushed a cup of tea across the pantry table to Keerthana, who had just cancelled her third client visit in a month.
'At twenty-five,' Ayesha said, 'I stopped taking lifts. Then trains. Then I stopped going anywhere I couldn't leave quickly. I read every self-help book in the library. Some helped for a week.
My sister finally said, "Ayesha, you've tried alone for a year. Let a doctor look at this with you." I was embarrassed. I thought only people in real trouble went.
The doctor listened and sent me to a therapist. It wasn't magic; it was months of small, planned steps. My sister never pushed. She drove me to the first few sessions and waited in the car with her crossword.'
Ayesha tapped the table. 'Asking early would have saved me a year.'

qa.q: What did young Ayesha stop taking first?
qa.a: She stopped taking lifts first.

qa.q: Why was young Ayesha embarrassed about seeing a doctor?
qa.a: She thought only people in real trouble went, so asking for help felt like admitting something shameful.

qa.q: What might Ayesha be hoping Keerthana will do next?
qa.a: She hopes Keerthana will ask a doctor or trained therapist early, since the cancelled visits suggest the fear is already limiting her work.

qa.q: What was the sister's part in Ayesha's recovery like?
qa.a: The sister was patient: she suggested a doctor, then drove Ayesha to sessions and waited with a crossword, supporting without pushing.

grounding: It shows, through a senior colleague's memory, how seeing a doctor and therapist helped when self-help was not enough, with a sister supporting patiently.

passage:
Trisha had tried everything on her own: breathing apps, journals, cold showers, a book on worry she had underlined twice. But the anxiety kept winning. She'd turned down a promotion because it involved travel, and last month she had left a friend's wedding halfway, heart hammering, sure she would faint.
When she finally decided to see someone, the first psychologist she called had a six-week waiting list, and her manager needed her for a product launch.
Devika, her friend since college, didn't lecture. She sat with her one evening and helped search: a clinic near the metro, an online therapist with evening slots, the family doctor as a first step. She didn't book anything for her. She just said, "I'll come with you to the first one if you want."
Trisha booked the family doctor for Saturday and a therapist for the following Tuesday evening, after work. Putting down the phone, she felt oddly relieved, as if she had set down a bag she'd been carrying alone.

qa.q: How long was the first psychologist's waiting list?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel after booking the appointments?
qa.a: She felt relieved, as if she had set down a heavy bag she'd carried alone.

qa.q: Why is Trisha's choice to see a doctor and therapist sensible?
qa.a: Self-help hadn't worked and anxiety was limiting her life, so qualified support is the wise next step.

qa.q: What might Devika feel helping without taking over?
qa.a: Devika is patient and caring, glad to help search while letting Trisha make the bookings herself.

grounding: Despite a waiting list and a busy job, a young woman whose anxiety limits her life books a doctor and therapist, with a patient friend's help.

passage:
For eight months Lalit had avoided the local train. He took two buses and an auto to his office in Andheri, leaving home at six-thirty to dodge the crowds. He'd skipped his cousin's engagement in Thane because it meant the train. He was tired all the time.
He had tried breathing exercises from videos and a planner full of positive sayings. Nothing touched it for long.
One night his sister Nirmala found him sitting on the stairs, sweating, after turning back at the station gate again. She didn't scold or offer tips. She said, "This has gone on long enough that you deserve proper help. Not just videos. Will you see a doctor? I'll sit in the waiting room, but you do the talking."
The next week Lalit saw their family doctor, who referred him to a psychologist. Walking out of the clinic, he felt embarrassed, and also something he hadn't felt in months: hopeful.

qa.q: How long had Lalit avoided the local train?
qa.a: For eight months.

qa.q: What did Lalit feel walking out of the clinic?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed but also hopeful for the first time in months.

qa.q: Why was seeing a doctor the right step for Lalit?
qa.a: The anxiety was limiting daily life and self-help hadn't worked, so a doctor and psychologist offer proper help.

qa.q: How does Nirmala help without taking over?
qa.a: Nirmala stays calm, suggests the doctor and offers to wait outside, while leaving the talking to Lalit.

grounding: A young man whose anxiety limits daily life moves from self-help to a doctor and psychologist, with his sister supporting patiently.

passage:
"I cancelled the therapist again," Sunaina said, pulling her knees up on the sofa.
"That's the second time," Nirmala said. "What happened?"
"I thought I could handle it myself. I've been doing the breathing thing."
"Is it helping?"
"For a bit. Then I still can't make myself go to the office on presentation days. I've taken four sick days this month."
"Four?"
"Don't. I know."
Nirmala sat down beside her. "I'm not going to push you. But it's been months, and it's getting in the way of your job. That's exactly when a trained person can help. Asking isn't weak. It's sensible."
"What if they think I'm overreacting?"
"Then they'll tell you. That's their job, not yours."
Sunaina was quiet. "Will you sit with me while I call to rebook?"
"Yes. You dial. I'll just be here."

qa.q: How many sick days has Sunaina taken this month?
qa.a: Four sick days this month.

qa.q: What is Sunaina afraid the therapist will think?
qa.a: She is afraid the therapist will think she's overreacting, which adds shame to her anxiety.

qa.q: Why is Nirmala's approach helpful?
qa.a: She is patient, explains that asking early is sensible, and sits beside Sunaina while letting her make the call.

qa.q: What might Nirmala feel hearing about the second cancellation?
qa.a: Nirmala feels concerned but steady, choosing not to push while clearly naming how far the anxiety reaches.

grounding: A young woman whose anxiety is affecting her job rebooks a therapist, with a friend who is patient and does not take over.

passage: I'm Sangeeta. For about a year I kept telling myself I'd fix the panic on my own. I watched breathing videos, bought a planner, did the lists. Some of it helped. But I was still avoiding the metro, still making excuses at work, and one day I realised I'd planned my whole week around not being in crowds. That was when I booked an appointment with a doctor, who referred me to a therapist. I was embarrassed at first, as if it meant I'd failed. It didn't. The therapist had tools I'd never have found alone. What surprised me most was Lavanya. She didn't take over or look things up for me. She just asked, every Friday, "Want company on the metro, or should I wait at the other end?" and let me choose. Some weeks I chose "other end."

qa.q: What did Lavanya ask every Friday?
qa.a: She asked: Want company on the metro, or should I wait at the other end?

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when booking the appointment?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed at first, as if asking for help meant failing, but later relieved to find it didn't.

qa.q: Why was seeing a doctor and therapist a sensible step for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Self-help helped only partly while fear was still shaping the whole week, and qualified support brought tools that could not be found alone.

qa.q: How did Lavanya help without taking over?
qa.a: Lavanya stayed patient and let Sangeeta choose each week whether to have company or be met at the other end, so control stayed with Sangeeta.

grounding: Shows a person seeing a doctor and therapist when anxiety keeps limiting daily life, with a friend helping patiently without taking over.
